text: Water is made of tiny pieces called molecules. Each molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. That is why we call it H2O. Water can be a liquid, a solid like ice, or a gas like steam. When you heat water, it turns into steam. When you cool it, it turns into ice.

Plants need sunlight, water, and air to grow. Their leaves catch sunlight and use it to make food. This is called photosynthesis. The roots drink water from the soil. Plants also take in a gas called carbon dioxide from the air and give out oxygen, which people and animals need to breathe.

Gravity is a force that pulls things toward each other. On Earth, gravity pulls people, balls, rain, and toys down toward the ground. When you jump, gravity pulls you back down. The Moon has gravity too, but it is weaker than Earth's gravity, so astronauts can jump higher there.

Animals live in places called habitats. A pond is a habitat for frogs and fish, while a forest is a habitat for birds, deer, and insects. A good habitat gives animals food, water, shelter, and space. If a habitat changes too much, some animals may need to move or may not survive.

All living things are made of cells. Some organisms like bacteria have just one cell, while humans have trillions. Each cell has a membrane that controls what goes in and out. Inside, the nucleus contains DNA, which carries genetic instructions. Mitochondria are organelles that produce energy by breaking down glucose through cellular respiration.

Natural selection is the process by which organisms with traits better suited to their environment tend to survive and reproduce more than others. Over many generations, this leads to changes in the characteristics of a population. Charles Darwin proposed this mechanism after observing finches on the Galapagos Islands, where different beak shapes had evolved to exploit different food sources.

Earth's outer shell is broken into large plates that move slowly over the softer mantle below. This movement is called plate tectonics. When plates collide, mountains can form. When they pull apart, magma can rise and create new crust. Earthquakes often happen where plates slide past each other along faults.

The periodic table organizes chemical elements by their atomic number, which is the number of protons in the nucleus. Elements in the same column often have similar properties because they have the same number of valence electrons. Metals appear mostly on the left, nonmetals on the right, and noble gases are stable elements in the last column.

The second law of thermodynamics states that the total entropy of an isolated system can only increase over time. Entropy measures the number of microscopic configurations consistent with a macroscopic state. In any spontaneous process, the universe moves toward greater disorder. This principle explains why heat flows from hot to cold objects and why perpetual motion machines are impossible.

Maxwell's equations unify electricity and magnetism into a single framework. A changing magnetic field induces an electric field, and a changing electric field induces a magnetic field. Together, these coupled fields propagate through space as electromagnetic waves traveling at the speed of light. This theoretical prediction, confirmed experimentally by Hertz, showed that light itself is an electromagnetic phenomenon.

Organic chemistry studies carbon-based molecules. Carbon can form four covalent bonds, creating chains, rings, and branched structures. Functional groups like hydroxyl, carboxyl, and amino groups determine a molecule's chemical behavior. These properties make carbon the backbone of all known life, from simple sugars to complex proteins and DNA.

Special relativity shows that the speed of light is the same for all observers regardless of their motion. This leads to time dilation: a moving clock ticks slower than a stationary one. It also implies mass-energy equivalence through E equals mc squared. These effects are negligible at everyday speeds but become significant near the speed of light.

In quantum mechanics, the state of a system is described by a wave function that evolves according to the Schrodinger equation. The Born rule interprets the squared modulus of the wave function as a probability density. Measurement collapses the wave function into an eigenstate of the observed operator, yielding a definite outcome with probability determined by the projection of the state onto that eigenstate.

The central limit theorem states that the sampling distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution as sample size increases, regardless of the population distribution, provided the variance is finite. This result underpins confidence intervals and hypothesis testing in frequentist statistics. The rate of convergence depends on the skewness and kurtosis of the underlying distribution, with the Berry-Esseen theorem providing explicit bounds.

General relativity describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy. The Einstein field equations relate the metric tensor to the stress-energy tensor through a system of ten coupled nonlinear partial differential equations. Solutions include the Schwarzschild metric for spherical masses and the Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker metric for cosmology.

Fourier analysis decomposes functions into sums of sinusoidal components. The Fourier transform maps a time-domain signal to its frequency-domain representation. For square-integrable functions, Parseval's theorem ensures that the total energy is preserved across domains. The discrete Fourier transform and its fast algorithm are foundational to digital signal processing.

A fiber bundle is a structure that locally looks like a product space but may have a different global topology. Formally, a fiber bundle consists of a total space E, a base space B, a fiber F, and a projection map that is locally trivial. The Mobius strip is a non-trivial line bundle over the circle. Principal bundles, where the fiber is a Lie group acting freely, are fundamental to gauge theory and the geometric formulation of Yang-Mills fields.

An adjunction between categories C and D consists of functors F: C to D and G: D to C together with a natural isomorphism between the hom-sets Hom(F(c), d) and Hom(c, G(d)) for all objects c in C and d in D. The functor F is called the left adjoint and G the right adjoint. Adjunctions encode universal properties and arise ubiquitously: free-forgetful pairs, tensor-hom, and the Galois connection between topology and algebra are all instances.

Homological algebra studies algebraic structures through chain complexes and their homology groups. A short exact sequence of chain complexes induces a long exact sequence in homology via the connecting homomorphism. Derived functors, constructed through projective or injective resolutions, measure the failure of a functor to preserve exactness. Ext and Tor are the prototypical examples, governing extensions and tensor products of modules.

Measure-theoretic probability builds on sigma-algebras and countably additive measures. The Radon-Nikodym theorem establishes the existence of density functions for absolutely continuous measures. Conditional expectation is defined as a projection onto a sub-sigma-algebra, and the martingale convergence theorem guarantees almost sure convergence for uniformly integrable martingales. These foundations support the rigorous treatment of stochastic processes and integration theory.
